title: What is the minimum annual salary in Australia? A complete guide for 2026–27
description: Find the minimum annual salary Australia for 2026–27. Learn how to convert hourly rates to annual pay, understand award wages, casual loading, tax, and super.
salarySummary: Based on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week, the minimum annual salary in Australia is approximately $52,254.80 before tax.

faqs.q: What is the minimum annual salary in Australia for 2026–27?
faqs.a: The minimum annual salary in Australia for an adult employee not covered by an award or agreement is based on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour. For a standard 38-hour week, that works out to $1,004.90 per week and $52,254.80 per year before tax. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making their minimum $33.05 per hour, or $65,318.50 annually. Most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then multiply by 52. For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,254.80. If you work part-time, use your actual weekly hours. You can also find your fortnightly pay by doubling the weekly amount.

faqs.q: Does the minimum annual salary include superannuation?
faqs.a: No. The minimum annual salary figures quoted are gross wages before tax. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at a rate of 12% (from 1 July 2026) up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So an employee earning the National Minimum Wage would also receive an additional $6,270.58 per year in super, bringing total employment cost to about $58,525.38.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the minimum annual salary in Australia

When you hear the term **minimum annual salary Australia**, it refers to the lowest amount an employer can legally pay an employee for a full year of work. This figure is derived from the National Minimum Wage set by the Fair Work Commission each year. For 2026–27, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, which translates to $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week, or **$52,254.80 per year** before tax and super. This rate applies to adult employees who are not covered by an award or registered agreement.

The Fair Work Ombudsman and the Fair Work Commission both confirm that the National Minimum Wage is the baseline. However, most Australian employees are covered by an industry or occupation award that sets higher minimum rates. You can check your award using the [pay guides](/blog) on our site or the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay and Conditions Tool.

## How to calculate your annual salary from an hourly rate

The basic formula is straightforward: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52**. For full-time employees, we assume a standard 38-hour week. For example:

- National Minimum Wage: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,254.80 per year
- Casual rate (with 25% loading): $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,318.50 per year

If you work part-time, use your actual weekly hours. You can also find your fortnightly pay by multiplying your weekly pay by 2. For the National Minimum Wage, that’s $2,009.80 per fortnight.

Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool does this calculation for you. Just enter your hourly rate and it shows annual, monthly, fortnightly, and weekly figures, with options to add casual loading.

## The National Minimum Wage and award rates

The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor, but awards often set higher rates. For example, the Hospitality Industry General Award or the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award have minimum rates above $26.44 per hour for most classifications. Always check your award first.

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the minimum wage to compensate for not receiving paid leave. This is included in the $33.05 per hour casual rate. The Fair Work Commission’s National Minimum Wage Order 2026 outlines the casual loading and special rates for juniors, apprentices, and employees with disability.

## Tax and super considerations

Your minimum annual salary is your gross pay before tax. For 2026–27, the Australian Tax Office resident tax rates are:
- $0–$18,200: nil
- $18,201–$45,000: 15%
- $45,001–$135,000: 30%
- $135,001–$190,000: 37%
- Over $190,000: 45%

A 2% Medicare levy generally applies. For the National Minimum Wage earner, tax and Medicare would be approximately $7,467 per year, leaving about $44,788 take-home pay. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a personalised estimate.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. So an employee on the minimum wage receives an extra $6,270.58 in super, making total employment cost $58,525.38. Super is not included in the annual salary figure quoted in job ads or award rates.

## Using our tools to find your pay

Our [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page explains the National Minimum Wage and special rates in detail. For award-specific pay, refer to the [pay guides](/blog) or the Fair Work Ombudsman’s resources. Remember that the figures on this site are estimates based on standard hours and do not include overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice.

## Key differences in ordinary-time earnings

While the minimum annual salary is $52,254.80, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that average full-time adult ordinary-time earnings were $2,083.70 per week in May 2026, or about $108,352 per year. That’s more than double the minimum. All employees total earnings (including part-time) averaged $1,579.20 per week, or $82,118 per year. These figures highlight the gap between minimum and average pay in Australia.

Understanding your minimum annual salary helps you negotiate fair pay and budget effectively. Whether you’re an employee checking your entitlements or an employer setting wages, knowing the legal minimum is the first step.
